title: Ginseng (Asian)
subtitle: The Chinese tonic root taken in cycles for sustained energy and cognitive support
excerpt: Panax ginseng is the flagship tonic root of Chinese medicine, used in the west as a strengthening herb taken in three-month cycles rather than continuously. Traditional Chinese, and secondary western use for fatigue and cognitive support. Carries firm cautions around pregnancy, high blood pressure, and anticoagulant medicines.

glossaryTerms.definition: The group of triterpenoid saponins unique to Panax species. Different ginsenosides have been studied for different effects; together they are considered responsible for most of ginseng's documented activity.
A herb used traditionally to strengthen and nourish over time rather than to address acute symptoms. Taken in cycles with rest periods, not continuously.

content.text: Asian ginseng in the home kitchen is the root preparation taken as a tonic herb in three-month cycles: a simmered preparation or an alcohol extract for sustained energy and mental clarity. Chinese medicine has used it as the primary tonic root for at least two thousand years. Western herbal practice adopted it in the twentieth century, where it found a home as a stress-supporting herb: a herb that helps the body manage sustained stress. Well-established evidence help the traditional cognitive-help use, especially in older adults. A alcohol extract stores for two years.
Precautions
Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor for ongoing or serious symptoms.
Pregnancy: do not use ginseng in pregnancy. Ginseng is avoided throughout pregnancy in all traditions that document it.

High blood pressure: ginseng is traditionally avoided in uncontrolled hypertension and in what Chinese medicine describes as heat conditions: high blood pressure, flushed complexion, and signs of internal heat. If you have hypertension or cardiovascular disease, speak to your prescriber before using ginseng.

Anticoagulant medicines: ginseng has mild antiplatelet activity. Readers on warfarin, aspirin, clopidogrel, or other blood-thinning medicines should consult their prescriber before using ginseng preparations.

Not for continuous long-term use: ginseng is a tonic herb used in cycles of three months on followed by one month off. Continuous daily use is not the traditional pattern in any source tradition and is not supported by the available evidence.
Botanical

Panax ginseng, family Araliaceae. The common name 'ginseng' covers several plants; Panax ginseng (also called Asian ginseng, Korean ginseng, or Chinese ginseng) is the primary species of the Chinese and Korean tradition. The genus name Panax means 'all-healing' in Greek, reflecting the root's broad traditional reputation. The part used is the root, harvested after at least four to six years of growth when the
ginsenosides

are at higher concentrations. The root is prepared as 'white ginseng' (dried and peeled) or 'red ginseng' (steamed and dried, which alters the ginsenoside profile). The plant is slow-growing, grows in shaded woodland, and is not practical to cultivate in most UK gardens. Wild-harvested ginseng is rare and expensive; cultivated root from reputable suppliers is the appropriate source.

American ginseng (Panax quinquefolius) is a separate species with a different compound profile. It is considered cooling in Chinese medicine and less stimulating than Asian ginseng. Siberian ginseng (Eleutherococcus senticosus) is not a true Panax. It is a different plant that shares only the common name.
active compounds and actions

Ginsenosides are the main active compounds in Panax ginseng. Over thirty have been found, with Rg1 and Rb1 the most studied. They work through steroid hormone receptors and influence the HPA (hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal) axis, which is the body's stress-response system. This is the mechanistic basis for the stress-supporting herb classification. The circulatory-stimulant action is linked to ginsenoside effects on nitric oxide production in blood vessel walls.
Traditional uses

Chinese medicine has used Panax ginseng root as the preeminent qi tonic for thousands of years. The classic application is to tonify qi (vitality), strengthen the spleen and stomach, calm the mind, and generate fluids. In practical terms, the Chinese tradition uses it for weakness and deficiency states: fatigue after illness. Poor appetite, palpitations from weakness, shortness of breath, and the specific pattern of qi deficiency. It is not a herb for everyone: it is suited to deficient and cold presentations, not to the robust and overheated. The traditional course structure of cycling with rest periods reflects the Chinese understanding of tonic herbs as something that must be integrated, not taken indefinitely.

Western herbal practice adopted ginseng in the twentieth century. It was framed as a stress-supporting herb: a herb that helps the body manage sustained physical and mental stress. The western uses centre on fatigue, sustained mental demand, and a sense of running on empty. Trial evidence supports the traditional use for cognitive function in older adults. Evidence for physical performance is more mixed.
Preparations

The traditional Chinese preparation is a simmered preparation of sliced root: simmer 1 to 3 g of dried root per cup in cold-start water, covered, for twenty minutes, then strain. The simmered preparation has a slightly sweet, earthy taste. It can be prepared as a larger batch for several days and kept in the fridge.

A alcohol extract in 40% spirit (1 part dried root to 5 parts spirit by weight. Macerated for four to six weeks) provides a more concentrated and standardised preparation. A standard dose from a alcohol extract is 1 to 2 ml in a small amount of water. Once or twice daily, taken in the morning rather than at bedtime because of its stimulating character.
Standardised extracts in capsule form are also widely available and have been used in most of the clinical trials. These provide the most consistent
ginsenoside
content but sit at the boundary between herbal preparation and supplement. Use them in the same cycling pattern as any other ginseng preparation.
Cautions and cautions
Pregnancy: ginseng is avoided throughout pregnancy in Chinese medicine and in western herbal practice. Do not use it during pregnancy.
High blood pressure: ginseng is not right for readers with high blood pressure. If you are on blood pressure medication, speak to your prescriber before using ginseng.
Anticoagulant medicines: ginseng has mild antiplatelet activity. It adds to the effect of warfarin and aspirin. Speak to your prescriber before combining.
Course length: use in three-month cycles with a one-month break between courses. Continuous indefinite use is not the traditional pattern and is not recommended.

Over-stimulation: some readers experience insomnia, agitation, or headache at the start of ginseng use, particularly if they are constitutionally warm or stressed. Start with a low dose and increase if well tolerated. If stimulation effects persist, ginseng may not be the right
tonic herb
for your constitution at this time.
